name: Q-switched / picosecond laser for dark circles

lead: Q-switched and picosecond lasers deliver extremely short, intense pulses of light. In dermatology they treat tattoos, dark spots and other pigmentation, and people apply the idea to periorbital hyperpigmentation, the brown-pigment type of dark circle, to lighten it.

Q-switching stores energy in the laser and releases it as one short pulse; in tattoo work the pulses shatter ink into particles the body clears, and the same physics is applied to pigment. Nd:YAG types are the most commonly favoured. A picosecond laser was introduced in 2013 for hard-to-remove inks. Periorbital hyperpigmentation is described as an inherited trait of extra melanin, most prevalent at ages 16 to 25. No published studies of these lasers for dark circles were located.

paras: Clinicians perform it in a clinic, typically as a series of sessions. It is discussed for pigment-type dark circles rather than those caused by hollows or visible vessels.
The sources reviewed do not discuss side effects. Periorbital skin is thin and close to the eye, so laser procedures there are done by clinicians.

angle.text: Users look to these dermatology pigment lasers to lighten brown-pigment dark circles. Short pulses break up pigment under the eye so the area looks lighter. The lasers are established for tattoos and pigmentation; published under-eye evidence is limited.

lead: Q-switched and picosecond lasers are short-pulse lasers that dermatologists use on tattoos and pigmentation. In appearance communities they are discussed as a way to lighten periorbital hyperpigmentation, the brown-pigment type of dark circle, so the skin under the eyes looks more even in tone and the face looks more rested.[1][2][2]

Q-switching builds up energy inside the laser and then releases it as a single, very short, intense pulse.[1] Q-switched lasers, with Nd:YAG types commonly favoured, are used for tattoo removal and for dark spots and other pigmentation problems.[1] Wikipedia dates the picosecond tattoo laser to 2013.[1] The pulses are meant to break pigment into particles that the body then clears.[1]

Dark circles have many causes, including thin skin showing blood vessels, hollowing, allergies and rubbing, and extra melanin around the eyes. Only the pigment type is the natural target for pigment lasers.[2][3] Dermatology literature discusses Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers for conditions such as melasma, lentigines and freckles, and a French review notes lasers are very effective for many hyperpigmented lesions but not for all kinds of pigmentation.[4][5]
infobox: Tattoo work typically takes many sessions at least a month apart[1]

paras: In active Q-switching an external switch controls release of stored laser energy; in passive Q-switching a saturable absorber does so. Compared with mode locking, Q-switching yields lower repetition rates and higher pulse energy.[1] In tattoo treatment, the pulses fragment ink particles that the lymphatic system clears, and full removal typically takes many sessions.[1]

Periorbital hyperpigmentation is described as an inherited trait of extra melanin, most prevalent at ages 16 to 25.[2] Wikipedia's overview of dark circles lists thin skin, bony structure, allergies, sun exposure, ageing and other contributors alongside pigment, and names lasers and intense pulsed light among specialist treatments.[3]

People who discuss under-eye darkness as a hardmaxxing topic list pigment lasers alongside peels, topical brighteners and microneedling as clinic options for the pigment type of dark circle. Hydroquinone, once common in lightening creams, has been restricted in Europe and lost over-the-counter approval in the US in 2006, according to Wikipedia.[3]

No studies found that test Q-switched or picosecond lasers specifically for under-eye dark circles in a reliable trial. A 2024 randomized trial that compared stromal vascular fraction, platelet-rich plasma and a 1064-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG laser for infraorbital dark circles has been retracted.[6]

Related research covers other pigmentation. A French review reports that lasers are a standard treatment for actinic lentigos and dermal hypermelanocytosis such as Ota nevus, that freckles and cafe-au-lait macules relapse almost constantly, and that Q-switched lasers at standard parameters are not recommended for melasma because of relapses and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[4] A 2009 trial of 45 Egyptian patients compared hydroquinone, trichloroacetic acid peels and frequency-doubled Q-switched Nd:YAG laser for melasma.[7] A 2024 randomized trial compared home-based 590 nm LED with in-hospital 1064 nm Q-switched Nd:YAG for facial melasma,[8] and a 2025 trial studied Q-switched Nd:YAG combined with medical therapy for hyperpigmentation.[9] A 2023 split-lesion trial compared picosecond and Q-switched 532 nm Nd:YAG lasers for ephelides (freckles).[10]

Dermatology reviews associate Q-switched lasers on melasma with relapse and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[4] The skin around the eyes is thin and close to the eye, which is why laser work in the area is performed by trained clinicians.[3]

timeline.event: Picosecond tattoo laser introduced, per Wikipedia.[1]
Randomized trial compares picosecond and Q-switched 532 nm lasers for freckles.[10]
